title: What Do I Wish My Leader Knew About Me
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on teacher Kyle Schwartz's well-known 'I wish my teacher knew ___' classroom exercise, this article translates the lesson from an elementary classroom to adult workplaces. Schwartz's third graders revealed hidden hardships — loneliness, poverty, anxiety — that changed how she taught; the author argues adults carry equivalent unseen struggles into work but rarely disclose them without an explicit invitation. The piece is careful to frame this awareness as a tool for adapting leadership style and timing, not for lowering standards or excusing performance. It closes with a practical suggestion: leaders should share their own backstory first to make disclosure feel reciprocal and safe.
points: A third-grade teacher's exercise ('I wish my teacher knew ___') revealed students' hidden struggles — loneliness, poverty, anxiety — that reshaped how she taught.
Adults carry the same hidden burdens into work that children carry into school, but rarely disclose them unless explicitly invited to.
Knowing team members' outside challenges isn't about lowering standards or making excuses — it's about adapting timing, tone, and approach to the person.
Leaders can unlock this kind of disclosure simply by sharing their own backstory first and asking without prying.
quotes: Several years ago, elementary school teacher Kyle Schwartz wrote “I wish my teacher knew _______” on the board and asked her 3rd-grade students to complete the sentence.
The revelations altered her entire approach to how she wanted to teach.
They learned that school children will share their realities with teachers if they are given the invitation.
Knowing what team members confront in their lives away from the workplace isn’t about compromising on work quality or making excuses for people.
Start by sharing your own backstory and asking them for theirs. What you learn might change how you lead.
